description: Records everywhere, the target rises to $124, BUY becomes HOLD, and the position enters the trim list
body_html:
What’s inside:

  • TLDR

  • How it ranks

  • The quarter: records everywhere

  • Thesis scorecard after Q2 2026

  • Guidance: raised, and still padded

  • Valuation: the target moves from $92 to $124

  • The risk register after Q2

  • Verdict

Since adding TPC to the portfolio, it is up almost 61%. I laid out the thesis in the September deep dive: a record backlog signed on better terms, minimal competition for mega-projects, margins inflecting, cash piling up, and a fair price offering a 53% upside.

Here in Toronto, I don’t think I have seen many TPC sites, but when I visited my brother in Manhattan, TPC was everywhere. For those that haven’t been there, Manhattan is in constant construction mode, so you always run into TPC.

TLDR

  • Record quarter. Revenue grew 19% y/y, operating income 54%, adjusted EPS 23%. Revenue and operating income were the highest of any quarter in TPC’s history.

  • 2026 adjusted EPS guidance was raised to $5.15-$5.45 after being affirmed “to remain conservative” in Q1. Management expects even higher earnings in 2027.

  • The July refinancing replaced an 11.875% coupon with 6.625%, saving $21M of cash interest a year. Net cash reached $473M, the dividend rose 50%, and TPC joined the S&P SmallCap 600.

  • Four thesis pillars confirmed, and the fifth, the valuation discount, has played out. The stock crossed my old $92 target.

  • Target moves from $92 to $124, and the rating moves from BUY to HOLD. TPC joins the trim list as the risk-reward profile is balanced (slightly negatively skewed).

How it ranks

Growth 97. The trailing columns are a turnaround in numeric form: diluted EPS growth of 192%, ROIC growth of 508%, EBITDA growth off a loss-making base. The forward columns drag the factor, and they mislead: the provider’s consensus is GAAP-based, and 2026 GAAP still carries the share-based compensation noise plus the one-time refinancing charge coming in Q3.

Valuation 45. The factor is split down the middle. The income statement looks expensive (41.8x trailing earnings, again the SBC distortion), while the cash engine looks cheap: 8.2x cash flow and 0.8x sales.

Profitability 73. ROIC of 15% and cash from operations near the top of the industrial universe carry the factor. Gross margin near 11.5% scores poorly against a 27.9% sector median.

Sentiment 91. Outlook 17. Momentum and revisions are strong; the Outlook factor reads the same distorted GAAP forward estimates the Growth factor does.

You can run this exact exercise on any ticker at RankedStocks.com, for free.

The quarter: records everywhere

Revenue grew 19% y/y, operating income grew 54%, and adjusted EPS grew 23%.

Revenue was the highest quarter ever…

… same for operating income.

Civil did the heavy lifting again. Revenue rose 11% to its highest quarter ever on the Midtown Bus Terminal, the Manhattan Tunnel, the Kensico-Eastview tunnel, the Honolulu rail project and the Apra Harbor repairs in Guam. The 15.3% operating margin sits above the top of management’s own 12-15% band for the year.

Operating income still fell y/y because Q2 2025 carried a $28M favourable settlement adjustment that made last year’s 19.1% margin unrepeatable. Read sequentially (12.6% in Q1 to 15.3% in Q2), the margin story is doing exactly what the thesis needs.

Building printed its best margin since 2012. Revenue grew 21% on the Brooklyn and Manhattan jails and a large healthcare campus in Northern California, and the 5.6% margin came near the top of the guided 3-6% band. Operating income was the best since 2010. For a segment I treated as filler in the original thesis, +39% income growth is a very good surprise.

Specialty completed the turnaround. Revenue grew 47% on the New York and Texas electrical and mechanical work, and the segment earned a 2.2% margin against a 10.2% loss a year ago (which included $14.6M of legacy claim settlements). Two-thirds of this backlog supports TPC’s own Civil and Building jobs, so the segment’s recovery compounds the others. Management still targets 5-8% eventually.

One caveat about the quarter. Consolidated gross margin fell to 12.9% from 14.3% because last year’s cost line was flattered by that Civil settlement, and the operating-income record got $26M of help from lower share-based compensation in G&A. The margin expansion is real, the y/y operating leverage overstates it.

Cash did what I said it would. First-half operating cash flow set a record at $334M, after full-year records in 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025. The CFO confirmed that only a small amount of it came from dispute resolutions. The old TPC generated cash by settling claims; this one generates it from operations. FCF for the half was $283M after capex, and the CFO expects the second half to trend toward a second-best-ever year.

Backlog held near record at $19.9B, a book-to-burn just over 1x in the quarter, though 6% below the $21.1B peak of a year ago. New awards of $1.7B included a $652M naval base power project in Guam, two Coast Guard projects in Alaska, extra funding for a Texas pediatric campus electrical job, a University of Mississippi building and a Minnesota bridge. The forward pipeline is the number that moved: more than $200B of prospective work over three to four years, three times the $70B-$90B range of the past several years (per the Q2 2026 earnings call Q&A). Management still expects $1B of additional Midtown Bus Terminal funding later this year, and Building has hundreds of millions in pre-construction, which historically converts to backlog more than 90% of the time.

Thesis scorecard after Q2 2026

Pillar #1. The record backlog converts into profitable revenue: Confirmed

Original thesis: the $21.1B backlog was signed on better terms than anything in TPC’s past, and Mr. Market refused to believe it would turn into earnings.

What happened since: 2025 revenue closed up 28%, the first half of 2026 is up another 15.5%, and Q2 revenue was the highest ever, driven by projects still in early execution with “significant scope of work remaining.”

Assessment: conversion is no longer a hypothesis, it is the income statement. The pillar holds even with backlog 6% off its peak, because burn is the point of backlog.

Pillar #2. Minimal competition for mega-projects: Confirmed

Original thesis: public competitors walked away from fixed-price mega-work, leaving TPC as the last big generalist; Ron Tutor claimed they rarely saw more than one other bidder.

What happened since: management repeated the observation this quarter (”we continue to see limited competition for the larger fixed-price work”) and keeps bidding selectively, with safe costs and contingency. In Guam, TPC is effectively the incumbent for the Pacific defence build-out, with $4.6B of Indo-Pacific opportunities identified over 12-18 months.

Assessment: intact. A $200B pipeline chased by few qualified bidders is the structural asymmetry that made me buy the stock, and it widened.

Pillar #3. Margin expansion: Confirmed and strengthening

Original thesis: newer contracts carried structurally better margins, visible first in Civil, later in Building and Specialty.

What happened since: Civil printed above its 12-15% band, Building near the top of its 3-6% band, Specialty went from losses to profit with management guiding further improvement in the second half.

Assessment: the strongest pillar this quarter. The CEO reminded everyone the Civil conversation used to be 8-12%; the bands themselves are migrating up.

Pillar #4. Cash generation and the balance sheet: Confirmed and strengthening

Original thesis: TPC had just reached net cash for the first time since 2010 ($107M), but carried an 11.875% bond I called pricey debt, and the bear case said the cash would sit idle.

What happened since: TPC swung from net debt to a net cash position in Q2 2025, the first time since 2010, and has widened it every quarter since.

The July refinancing replaced the 11.875% notes with $400M of 6.625% notes due 2033, saving $21M of cash interest annually, and the revolver doubled to $350M at far tighter spreads. The dividend rose 50% to $0.09 a quarter, buybacks continue with $170M authorized, and the pension plan was terminated. The S&P SmallCap 600 added the stock in July.

Assessment: the idle-cash worry got answered with a capital-returns programme. Note the one-time cost: Q3 will absorb a $51M debt-extinguishment charge, excluded from adjusted EPS.

Pillar #5. The market pays for none of it: Played out

Original thesis: at $60 the stock traded at a single-digit multiple of FCF and 0.69x trailing EV/Sales against a $92 DCF value.

What happened since: Mr. Market changed his mind. The stock crossed $92 in the spring and again in July, and at $97 it trades near 18x the midpoint of this year’s adjusted EPS guidance and 9.5x this year’s EBITDA in my model.

Assessment: at the deep dive, the gap to fair value was +53% with net cash as the floor. Today the gap to my new $124 target is +28%, against -38% to my $60 bear case. That is a 1 to 0.73 risk-reward: balanced, where the deep dive setup was heavily tilted in my favour. The discount that made this a top pick no longer exists, which is a compliment to the thesis and the main reason it is going from Buy to Hold.

Guidance: raised, and still padded

Management raised 2026 adjusted EPS guidance to $5.15-$5.45 from $4.90-$5.30, having affirmed the original range in Q1 while admitting on that call they “did consider raising guidance because we feel better about our position, but we want to be prudent.” The supporting assumptions all moved favourably: less G&A, less interest after the refinancing, a lower tax band.

On credibility: this team guided 2025 conservatively and raised twice, affirmed 2026 in May when it could have raised, then raised in August. Every guide since 2024 has carried “a significant amount of contingency,” their words, and the CEO went further in the Q&A: the nine mega projects are all ahead of cost on cash, and there is “more profit in those projects than what we are recognizing currently.” I treat the new range as a floor with the usual caveat that fixed-price construction can humble anyone.

One more item deserves its own paragraph: the extraordinary share-based compensation. TPC’s long-term incentive awards are liability-classified, so the expense is re-measured against the share price every quarter, and a stock that rises 60% in a year inflates the SBC. SBC cost $1.08 per diluted share in the first half of 2026, and it is why GAAP earnings have run close to $2 below adjusted since 2025. The mechanics are already unwinding: part of the awards vested at the end of 2025 (Q2 SBC halved y/y), most of the rest vest at the end of 2026, and the CFO expects the expense to be sharply lower in 2027; the G&A guide already came down for that reason. Based on that commentary, I treat it as a one-off, the cost of the share price exploding, and it means the GAAP vs adjusted gap mostly closes on its own next year.

Valuation: the target moves from $92 to $124

I updated the model with 2025 actuals and rebuilt the forecast assumptions. Four items changed.

You can check the model here.

First, the base is bigger. The September 2025 model assumed 2025 revenue of $5.28B; TPC printed $5.54B. My 2026 build now compounds +17.6% on top of that (Civil +15%, Building +16%, Specialty +30%, each below its first-half exit rate), then +13% in 2027 as the mega projects hit full construction. The old model had 13% and 11% for those years.

Second, the margin path moved up before fading. Near years hold the segments inside management’s guided bands (Civil printing above 12-15%, Building at the top of 3-6%, Specialty crawling toward 5-8%), then fade Civil back to its 10-year average by the terminal year. The fade discipline from the deep dive stays; the starting point rose.

Third, money got cheaper. The refinancing cuts interest expense to $42-44M this year and to $29M from 2027. The model now discounts at a 7.6% WACC (10.4% cost of equity from a 1.4 beta, 4.7% risk-free and 4.2% market risk premium, blended with a 40% debt weighting) vs. 9.3% at the deep dive, when the balance sheet still carried an 11.875% coupon.

Fourth, the share count finally bends down. Buybacks ran at $30M in the first half at an average near $72, with $170M authorized.

The DCF lands at $124 per share, up from $92.

What does $97 imply? Strip the $473M of net cash and the market is paying 9.5x this year’s EBITDA and 16x next year’s earnings for a business guiding double-digit growth in both. That is a fair price for a good contractor, and TPC has spent seven quarters proving it is one. It is no longer a mispriced one. To get much above my $124 you need the pipeline to convert into a new backlog record at today’s margins, which is possible (Sepulveda alone is a $12B programme, Newark Terminal B is $3B, and the BUILD America 250 Act proposes $580B of surface-transportation reauthorization), but that is the bull case, and I don’t pay for bull cases in advance.

The bear case is $60: backlog conversion stalls, Civil mean-reverts to its 10-year average margin, and you are left holding 12x $5 of earnings power, with the balance sheet limiting the damage. Having said that, the floor under this bear case is far sturdier than the one under the $5 stock of 2022; the company would still be net cash and paying a dividend.

The risk register after Q2

Execution at scale. Nine mega projects worth $16B running simultaneously is the largest concurrent programme in TPC’s history. Everything management sees is positive, revenue recognition is deliberately conservative, and Ron Tutor still reviews the big jobs. The risk is unchanged in kind, larger in exposure.

Litigation. One risk faded and one materialized. The Alaskan Way Viaduct saga, the defining lawsuit of the past decade, settled and was dismissed in June with all matters resolved. Against that, a Philadelphia court awarded a developer $175M in April over the W/Element hotel project; TPC filed its appeal on July 7 and carries only an immaterial charge, so if the award survives appeal in full the hit would be near $3.3 per share pre-tax, and Mr. Market has not priced it. Costs in excess of billings, my red-flag line from the deep dive, sit at $846M: claims are flat, but unapproved change orders grew $40M this half (Q2 2026 10-Q).

The funding cliff. The Bipartisan Infrastructure Law’s obligation window closes September 30, 2026. Its proposed successor is in committee, and 73% of backlog is state and local money, largely voter-approved, so existing projects are funded; the risk is to the pace at which the $200B pipeline converts, not to the work in hand.

Verdict

I am moving TPC from BUY to HOLD, with the target rising from $92 to $124. The position keeps its place in the portfolio for now, and it goes onto the trim list: the risk and the reward profile is slightly negatively skewed. The multiple has done its re-rating; from here the earnings have to do the work, project by project, and I’m happy to be paid the new dividend while they do.

If this update was useful, share it with a friend who invests.
